item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Fliegen in und ab Deutschland hat sich in den vergangenen Jahren massiv verteuert. Der durchschnittliche Ticketpreis habe sich zwischen 2010 und 2024 von knapp unter 150 Euro auf rund 300 Euro etwa verdoppelt, erklärten der Bundesverband der Deutschen Luftverkehrswirtschaft (BDL) und das Deutsche Zentrum für Luft- und Raumfahrt (DLR) am Montag in einem ersten gemeinsamen Bericht zur Lage der Branche. Grund seien neben stark gestiegenen staatlichen Abgaben wie Luftverkehrsteuer, Luftsicherheitsabgaben und Flugsicherungsgebühren auch höhere Personal- und Betriebskosten. Die Ticketpreise in Europa hätten im Schnitt von fast 250 Euro auf knapp 340 Euro zugelegt. Derzeit treffe die Airlines und die ganze Branche der wegen des Iran-Kriegs hohe Ölpreis stark, sagte BDL-Hauptgeschäftsführer Joachim Lang. "Der Kerosinpreis zerstört nochmal sämtliche Wirtschaftlichkeitsrechnungen." Fluglinien hätten einen doppelten Schaden - etwa auf dem Weg nach Asien müssten sie wegen anhaltender Luftraumsperrungen zwei Stunden länger fliegen und deshalb ohnehin mehr tanken. Zusätzlich sorge nun das [USN:L8N45L0AC TEXT:"teure Kerosin"] für eine weitere Belastung. DEUTSCHE DREHKREUZE VERLIEREN - TÜRKEI & GOLFREGION GEWINNEN "Der Report zeigt eine schleichende Abkopplung Deutschlands vom internationalen Luftverkehr", erklärte Lang. "Verbindungen fallen weg, Passagiere und Fracht weichen auf Drehkreuze außerhalb Europas aus." Für eine Exportnation sei das ein ernstes Standortproblem. Im Luftverkehr zeigen sich demnach seit 2010 deutliche Verschiebungen beim Umsteigen und bei Drehkreuzen. So verlagerten sich Passagierströme im Langstreckenverkehr zunehmend auf Hubs außerhalb der Europäischen Union, vor allem in der Türkei und der Golfregion. "Zwischen Deutschland und Fernost-/Südostasien stieg der Anteil der Verbindungen über Nicht-EU-Drehkreuze von 34 auf 54 Prozent", heißt es im Bericht. Zugleich sei der Anteil über deutsche Drehkreuze von 56 auf 36 Prozent gefallen. Ähnliches zeige sich im Luftverkehr nach Afrika. Die deutsche Luftfahrt-Lobby kritisiert seit langem, dass staatlich subventionierte Airlines aus der Türkei und den Golfstaaten deutliche Vorteile hätten. LUFTFAHRT-BOOM - ABER KAUM WACHSTUM IN DEUTSCHLAND Die weltweite Zahl der Flugreisenden steigt nach Prognosen des DLR bis 2034 - auch dank größerer und effizienterer Flugzeuge - auf 154 Prozent des Vor-Corona-Niveaus von 2019. Bei den Verbindungen zwischen Deutschland und Europa werde der Stand aus der Zeit vor der Virus-Pandemie noch nicht wieder erreicht. "Die Menschen wollen fliegen", sagte Lang und sprach von einem globalen Luftfahrt-Boom. "Die schlechte Nachricht ist: Dieses Wachstum findet zunehmend ohne Deutschland statt." Rund 536.900 Arbeitsplätze standen 2024 direkt oder indirekt mit der Luftfahrt in Zusammenhang, wie aus dem Report hervorgeht. Demnach schufen Luftverkehrswirtschaft und Luftfahrtindustrie in Deutschland eine Bruttowertschöpfung von 58,4 Milliarden Euro. Damit trug die Branche etwa 1,3 Prozent zum deutschen Bruttoinlandsprodukt bei.

item.title: Afghan Taliban says problems with Pakistan can be resolved through diplomacy
item.description: Problems affecting relations between neighbours Afghanistan and Pakistan can be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy, Afghan Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi said on Monday at talks on Afghanistan held in Moscow.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Problems affecting relations between neighbours [USN:L8N45G0JB TEXT:"Afghanistan and Pakistan"] can be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy, Afghan Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi said on Monday at talks on Afghanistan held in Moscow. Instead of seeking "political understanding", Pakistan's powerful military uses only military language in relations with Afghanistan and has carried out aggression in violation of international laws, Muttaqi said Kabul considers self-defence against any aggression to be its legitimate and undeniable right, Muttaqi added Pakistan’s foreign ministry, in a statement, said its representative at the event vowed to uproot terrorism from across the border, and called on the Taliban to end the "impunity with which terrorist groups continue to operate from their soil". Pakistan and Afghanistan have been at odds over militancy, with Islamabad accusing Kabul of harbouring militants who stage cross-border attacks The Taliban government denies the charge and says militancy is Pakistan's internal problem

item.title: US and German scientists win Nobel medicine prize for work on light and brain
item.description: American Karl Deisseroth and Germans Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine on Monday for developing optogenetics, a technique that uses light to control individual nerve cells in the brain.
item.dc:creator: Johan Ahlander, Marie Mannes, Bhanvi Satija
item.content:encoded: American Karl Deisseroth and Germans Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine on Monday for developing optogenetics, a technique that uses light to control individual nerve cells in the brain. The Nobel Assembly of Sweden's Karolinska Institute said Deisseroth, 54, Hegemann, 71, and Nagel, 73, had been selected for their "discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics." "This method (optogenetics) makes it possible to switch on, or off, the activity of individual nerve cells in a living brain," said Thomas Perlmann, Secretary-General of the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet. Anna Wedell, a professor in genetics and a member of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine, said a new era in neuroscience had opened but it was only the beginning. "For the first time we can actually start to understand how the brain processes information and how different neurons interact across the brain," she said. The trio will share a prize sum of 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million). [USN:L1N45N0AY TEXT:"Announcements"] will follow in the coming days on this year's Nobel physics, chemistry, literature, peace and economics prizes, with the winner or winners of the 2026 [USN:L6N45F0CZ TEXT:"Nobel Peace Prize"] to be announced on Friday. Deisseroth said he was still awake in the early hours when he was called from Stockholm. "I was not yet asleep, being a night owl, and now I don't think I'll be able to sleep for quite a while," he said. BREAKTHROUGH FROM ALGAE Deisseroth was training to become a neurosurgeon when he encountered patients he could not help at a psychiatric clinic. That encounter — witnessing suffering he had no tools to treat — prompted a question that would define his career: Why does the brain work so differently in different people? The answer would come from an unexpected place: an alga, and two German scientists driven by equally simple curiosity. Hegemann, fascinated by exploration and unknown territory, began investigating in the early 1990s how the alga Chlamydomonas reacts to light in half a millisecond. He hypothesized that a single protein both captured light and acted as an ion channel. Nagel tested this hypothesis by injecting Chlamydomonas genes into frog eggs, discovering channelrhodopsin-2 — a light-sensitive ion channel. In 2003, Nagel and Hegemann published findings showing the protein could be introduced into human cells to generate electrical impulses using light. Deisseroth showed the technique in rat nerve cells in 2005, and the method was named optogenetics in 2006. One scientist at Hegemann's Max Planck Institute in Frankfurt in 2007 recalled researchers taping optical fibers salvaged from Christmas decorations to microscopes. "We didn't really know how it worked. We didn't really have any tools," said Dima Kuzmin, a neurochemist at the time. "And it was massively exciting." TREATMENTS UNDER DEVELOPMENT The three laureates' research is now providing insights about brain disorders. Animal models are being used to understand schizophrenia, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, epilepsy and addiction — conditions that affect millions of people worldwide and have limited treatment options. Deisseroth used optogenetics to control the movements of mouse whiskers by activating specific nerve cells in the motor cortex. He also used light to wake sleeping mice, confirming that specific nerve cells control wakefulness. "There are mouse models of dementia, epilepsy, addiction. By understanding which cells are active in these diseases in mice, we can understand where to look in humans," Wedell said. Researchers are also applying the technique to try to restore vision to people blinded by retinitis pigmentosa — a progressive eye disease — by inserting a light-sensitive protein into the retina. They also hope optogenetics could improve cochlear implants, potentially allowing more precise stimulation of the auditory nerve than current electrical devices. "When you think about it in the retina, all patients need to do is open their eyes and you have the light. So it makes a lot of sense as a potential therapy," said Paul Bresge, CEO of US biotechnology company Ray Therapeutics, which is developing a therapy to treat retinitis pigmentosa. The most advanced of the treatments are autism spectrum disorder therapy by a US-based biotech company MapLight, co-founded by Deisseroth, and a vision restoration medicine for retinitis pigmentosa by Nanoscope, also based in the United States, though both are still some way from reaching patients. Manuel Valero, researcher at Barcelona-based Hospital del Mar, where he heads the Neural Computation Laboratory, said optogenetics had "allowed us to push the boundaries between science and science fiction." "In laboratory animals, we have managed to control emotions, create false memories or even recover lost memories in models of Alzheimer’s disease," Valero said. "Perhaps the great promise it has yet to fulfil is precisely one of its founding promises: its ability to treat diseases of the human brain." Each laureate's path reflected their distinct character. Hegemann developed an early fascination with exploration, viewing scientific research as charting unknown territory. Nagel had worked as a teacher, opened a cafe and taken up hang gliding as a hobby. The suffering witnessed by Deisseroth at the psychiatric clinic drove him to seek deeper understanding of the brain through research rather than clinical practice alone.

item.title: Yemeni government forces advance to Bab el-Mandeb Strait
item.description: Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces have secured effective control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, Yemen's Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani told Reuters on Monday, though fighting continues with Houthi forces in the area.
item.dc:creator: Mohammed Ghobari, Timour Azhari
item.content:encoded: Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces have secured effective control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, Yemen's Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani told Reuters on Monday, though fighting continues with Houthi forces in the area. The [USN:L1N45Q02D TEXT:"government forces"] advanced rapidly along the coast with heavy [USN:L8N45M1W0 TEXT:"Saudi air support"] to seize key positions in the Dhubab area on the narrowest point of the strait, a vital oil route whose seizure by the [USN:L1N45Q02Z TEXT:"Iran-backed Houthis"] last month sent shockwaves through energy markets. However, while Eryani said the military had seized Dhubab airstrip, located just inland from [USN:L8N4520BL TEXT:"the strait"], and cut off remaining Houthi forces in the area, another government source said fighting continued at a military base near the strait. The Houthis earlier denied that government forces had made gains, describing such claims as "completely untrue", and they threatened to attack any aircraft flying in Saudi airspace. While recapturing the coastal area around the strait would make it harder for the Houthis to disrupt shipping between the Mediterranean and Indian Ocean, they could still target vessels with drones from positions further up the coast and inland. Meanwhile, the Houthis themselves made important advances near the city of Taiz, gaining sections of a mountain road to leave government forces there besieged, according to five military sources with the Yemeni government. One other government source denied the road had been cut. KEY ENERGY EXPORT ROUTE UNDER THREAT Fighting has raged along several frontlines in Yemen for weeks after a dormant civil war erupted in a spillover from the US-Iran conflict , with the Houthis seeking to control the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait and firing missiles and drones at Saudi cities and infrastructure. With Gulf energy exports already restricted by Iran's closure of the Hormuz Strait, the fighting in Yemen has threatened another major oil export route, pushing up global prices and raising new risks in a region already aflame. The renewed fighting has worsened a humanitarian crisis in Yemen, with the UN migration agency saying on Monday that some 184,000 people had now been displaced since the war resumed. The internationally recognised Yemeni government announced on Sunday the launch of its offensive to recapture territory, with President Rashad al-Alimi swearing to fight "until the country is liberated from the grip of the terrorist militia". Saudi Arabia, which arms and trains Yemeni government forces, is backing the military campaign with air power and has sought logistical help from allies to push back the Houthis, restore free traffic in the Red Sea, and end the group's attacks on its territory. Riyadh said on Monday it had attacked hundreds of targets in Yemen to provide air cover for the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and Yemeni ground forces. The Yemeni government said it had launched attacks on several fronts including in the province of Sanaa, the Yemeni capital. The Houthi-run health ministry said two people had been killed and seven wounded in strikes on Sanhan and Sa'wan districts in Sanaa province. HEAVIEST FIGHTING IS IN SOUTHWEST YEMEN While the war has raged on several frontlines in Yemen, the heaviest fighting has been in the southwest, both in the coastal area near the strait and in the hills around Taiz, where the Houthis have been battling to surround government forces. Last week Houthi attacks damaged a culvert on the Taiz-Aden road, making it impassable. On Sunday night the group's fighters made new advances into the town of al-Turbah, sitting atop a high promontory on the road, five government military sources said, though another government source denied this. A Houthi-run news agency on Monday cited a military source as saying the group had driven government forces from the al-Mawasit district of Taiz province, reaching the home of Alimi, head of Yemen's interim presidential council. Those fresh advances leave Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city with a population of over half a million and a garrison of thousands of government fighters, surrounded by Houthi forces, the government military sources said. Taiz, nestled among Yemen's southern highlands, has been on the frontlines since early in the civil war, often under Houthi shell and sniper fire. In al-Mudhaffar area, just outside Taiz but within the area besieged by the Houthis, a long queue formed outside a petrol station on Monday as people waited for fuel and cooking gas canisters. "This is the daily state in Taiz. The suffering of citizens continues in this state," said one man queuing, Shehab Hazaa. Yemen's conflict began after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in the following year with an air campaign aimed at restoring the government and ousting the Iran-backed group. The fighting quickly ground to a bloody stalemate, with most frontlines stalled, leading to a major humanitarian crisis in what was already the poorest Arab state, until a ceasefire was agreed in 2022 that held until this summer.

item.title: Las fuerzas gubernamentales yemeníes avanzan hacia el estrecho de Bab el-Mandeb
item.description: Las fuerzas del Gobierno yemení, respaldadas por Arabia Saudita, han conseguido el control efectivo del estrecho de Bab el-Mandeb, según declaró el lunes a Reuters el ministro de Información de Yemen, Moammar al-Eryani, aunque continúan los combates con las fuerzas hutíes en la zona.
item.dc:creator: Mohammed Ghobari, Timour Azhari
item.content:encoded: Las fuerzas del Gobierno yemení, respaldadas por Arabia Saudita, han conseguido el control efectivo del estrecho de Bab el-Mandeb, según declaró el lunes a Reuters el ministro de Información de Yemen, Moammar al-Eryani, aunque continúan los combates con las fuerzas hutíes en la zona. Las fuerzas gubernamentales avanzaron rápidamente a lo largo de la costa con un fuerte apoyo aéreo saudí para hacerse con posiciones clave en la zona de Dhubab,en el punto más estrecho del estrecho. La ruta petrolera vital fue capturada el mes pasado por los hutíes, respaldados por Irán, en una acción que causó una gran conmoción en los mercados energéticos. Eryani afirmó que el ejército se había hecho con la pista de aterrizaje de Dhubab, situada justo en el interior del estrecho, y había aislado a las fuerzas hutíes que quedaban en la zona, pero otra fuente del Gobierno señaló que los combates continuaban en una base militar cercana al estrecho. Los hutíes habían negado antes que las fuerzas gubernamentales hubieran logrado avances, calificando tales afirmaciones de "completamente falsas", y amenazaron con atacar a cualquier aeronave que sobrevolara el espacio aéreo saudí. Aunque la reconquista de la zona costera en torno al estrecho dificultaría a los hutíes la interrupción del tráfico marítimo entre el Mediterráneo y el Océano Índico, estos aún podrían atacar a los buques con drones desde posiciones más al norte de la costa y en el interior. Mientras tanto, los propios hutíes lograron avances importantes cerca de la ciudad de Taiz, donde se hicieron con tramos de una carretera de montaña, dejando allí a las fuerzas gubernamentales sitiadas, según cinco fuentes militares del Gobierno yemení. Otra fuente gubernamental desmintió que se hubiera cortado la carretera. RUTA CLAVE Los combates se han recrudecido en las últimas semanas, tras el estallido de una guerra civil latente como consecuencia del conflicto entre Estados Unidos e Irán, en la que los hutíes buscan controlar Bab el-Mandeb y lanzan misiles y drones contra ciudades e infraestructuras saudíes. Como las exportaciones energéticas del golfo Pérsico ya se ven restringidas por el cierre del estrecho de Ormuz por parte de Irán, los combates en Yemen han puesto en peligro otra importante ruta de exportación petrolera, provocando un aumento de los precios mundiales y generando nuevos riesgos en una región ya en llamas. La reanudación de los combates ha agravado la crisis humanitaria en Yemen. La agencia de la ONU para las migraciones afirmó el lunes que unas 184.000 personas se han visto desplazadas desde que se reanudó la guerra. El Gobierno yemení reconocido internacionalmente anunció el domingo el inicio de su ofensiva para recuperar territorio, y el presidente Rashad al-Alimi juró luchar "hasta que el país sea liberado de las garras de la milicia terrorista". Arabia Saudita, que arma y entrena a las fuerzas gubernamentales, está respaldando la campaña militar con apoyo aéreo y pidió ayuda logística a sus aliados para hacer retroceder a los hutíes, restablecer la libre circulación en el mar Rojo y poner fin a los ataques del grupo contra su territorio. Riad afirmó el lunes que había atacado cientos de objetivos en Yemen para proporcionar cobertura aérea al estrecho y a las fuerzas terrestres yemeníes. El Gobierno yemení afirmó que había lanzado ataques en varios frentes, entre ellos en la provincia capitalina de Saná. El Ministerio de Salud, controlado por los hutíes, afirmó que dos personas fallecieron y otra siete resultaron heridas en los ataques contra los distritos de Sanhan y Sa'wan, en la provincia de Saná.

item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Der Dax (.GDAXI) ist kaum verändert in die neue Woche gestartet. Für gedämpfte Stimmung trotz einer Stabilisierung am Öl- und Anleihemarkt sorgte am Montag laut Experten ein erneuter Rückgang beim Euro. Der Dax notierte zur Eröffnung knapp im Plus bei 25.251,39 Punkten. Am [USN:L8N45O1AZ TEXT:"Freitag"] hatte er dank Hoffnungen auf eine lockerere Geldpolitik der US-Notenbank Fed nach schwachen US-Arbeitsmarktdaten den besten Handelstag seit zwei Monaten verzeichnet. Die europäische Gemeinschaftswährung büßte gut ein halbes Prozent auf 1,1186 Dollar ein. Seit Ende August beläuft sich das Minus auf rund 3,7 Prozent. "Deutsche Landtagswahlen, die auf einen politischen Umbruch hindeuten, Massenproteste und mögliche Neuwahlen in Spanien, die Zwischenwahlen in den USA und die französischen Wahlen im Frühjahr - im nächsten halben Jahr wird man als Anleger an dem Thema Politik nicht vorbeikommen", sagte Jochen Stanzl, Chefanalyst der Consorsbank. Dabei sei der Absturz des Euro für den Dax "Segen und Fluch": Die meisten Unternehmen im Index profitierten zwar durch bessere Exportaussichten von einer Währungsabwertung. Gleichzeitig trage sie jedoch zu einer bereits bestehenden politischen Unsicherheit bei, die internationale Investoren europäische Aktien vermeiden lässt. Bei den Einzelwerten zogen die Aktien der Rüstungsfirmen Rheinmetall (RHMG.DE) und Hensoldt (HAGG.DE) um jeweils rund 1,5 Prozent an. Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz hat der Ukraine bei einem Überraschungsbesuch am Sonntag ein umfangreiches [USN:L8N45R02G TEXT:"Hilfspaket"] angeboten. Die ukrainische Regierung und ukrainische Firmen vereinbarten mit deutschen Rüstungskonzernen nach Angaben der Bundesregierung 14 Kooperationen mit einem Gesamtvolumen von rund 6,6 Milliarden Euro. Nach oben ging es auch für die Aktien des Reifenherstellers Continental (CONG.DE) , die sich mit einem Plus von gut zwei Prozent an die Spitze des Dax setzten. Die Experten der US-Investmentbank Morgan Stanley hatten die Titel auf "Overweight" nach zuvor "Equal Weight" hochgestuft.

item.title: EU risks becoming sick man of the world if it doesn’t reform quickly
item.description: Time is running out for the European Union to deliver the economic reforms set out by former European Central Bank chief Mario Draghi two years ago. If the bloc fails, it faces the prospect of long-term comparative decline, becoming an also-ran on the world stage.
item.dc:creator: Mike Peacock
item.content:encoded: Time is running out for the European Union to deliver the [USN:L1N3YH0TV TEXT:"economic reforms"] set out by former European Central Bank chief Mario Draghi two years ago. If the bloc fails, it faces the prospect of long-term comparative decline, becoming an also-ran on the world stage. The bloc set the end of 2027 as its deadline for delivering key elements of Draghi’s blueprint, which include a complete single market featuring capital markets and energy unions, more common borrowing and fewer requirements for unanimous member state support for major reforms. As of July, the European Union had delivered on only 15.7% of Draghi’s proposals in full, with about a further 40% partially tackled, according to the European Policy Innovation Council. If you zero in on the most radical – and thus the most important – measures such as single capital and energy markets, the picture is even worse. The EU has successfully legislated on just 3% of those, according to French think tank Institut Montaigne. The European Commission can only push through these with all member states’ agreement – a daunting task. Europe’s upcoming election calendar could make that much harder. Governments facing voters are unlikely to be keen to relinquish more sovereignty, and if these elections produce less reform-minded leaders, the fabric of EU integration could start to unravel. HEADING TO THE POLLS France is in the spotlight with elections in April. The EU is already scrambling to finalise the bloc’s next long-term budget, covering 2028-2034, before these polls for fear that they could deliver a far-right government headed by [USN:L1N45507C TEXT:"Marine Le Pen."] While Le Pen’s National Rally has abandoned its ambition to leave the EU, it has still indicated that it wants to curb France’s contribution to the bloc’s budget and opt out of key parts of energy policy, while reimposing border controls. Meanwhile, Spain is now coming to the polls sooner than expected. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Monday called an [USN:L8N45R05A TEXT:"early election"] for November 29 after parliament rejected the government's housing decrees last week amid significant public protests. Votes in Italy and Poland come later in 2027. They could further complicate reform efforts as leaders may be loath to support potentially prudent reform measures, which require relinquishing national sovereignty, right before going to the polls. Then there is Germany. While the country’s ruling coalition is in power until 2029, surging support for the far-right [USN:L8N4591XZ TEXT:"Alternative for Germany"] (AfD) – which has supported [USN:S8N44V0A2 TEXT:"closer ties with Russia"] and severe immigration restrictions – could stall reform efforts in the bloc’s largest economy. Germany, under Chancellor Friedrich Merz, has, up until now, been more ambitious in its reform agenda than most of its neighbours. Since taking office last year, he has loosened Germany’s [USN:L1N3ZH03Y TEXT:"“debt brake”"] – a fiscal rule that had long stymied growth – to allow for sharply higher defence spending and the creation of a €500 billion infrastructure fund. This was followed up with plans to upgrade the country’s electricity grid alongside pension, tax and labour reforms. The spending has been popular, but [USN:L8N4340M1 TEXT:"reform measures"], such as cracking down on workers’ sick days and welfare abuse, and gradually raising the state pension age, emphatically are not – as evidenced by recent election results. “The main takeaway is that Germans don’t want reforms and want to stay either in a never-changing present or return to the past,” wrote Carsten Brzeski, chief economist at ING, after the ruling Christian Democratic Union (CDU) suffered heavy losses in [USN:L8N45D0G1 TEXT:"regional elections"] amid the surge in support for the AfD. While the AfD has yet to win any governing majorities and should struggle to find coalition partners, its rapid rise in the past decade to become Germany’s highest-polling party cannot be dismissed – especially as its popularity could push the ruling party to slow down on reforms that appear to reduce national sovereignty. ACID TESTS A palpable sense of urgency is present among EU officials. “Where projects are in Europe's strategic interests, we need to massively accelerate,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said last month in her annual "State of the Union" address to the European Parliament. Nevertheless, there appears to be little appetite for pooling power. Draghi’s call for more euro zone common borrowing already looks dead in the water. The key tests will now be whether EU leaders can deliver a savings and investment union as well as an energy union. Creating a single capital market could help the bloc tap the €35 trillion in EU household savings, which are dispersed across the 27 member states and often invested abroad. A parallel drive to simplify a fragmented regulatory system could also yield significant gains. The International Monetary Fund's analysis in April estimated the reform agenda could raise European productivity by 20% over a decade, though that projection does rely on several optimistic assumptions. A key component of this competitiveness agenda is [USN:L1N43F0ZC TEXT:"energy reform."] The European Central Bank estimates that rapid adoption of AI could lift EU productivity by up to 4% over a decade. However, building and running data centres and AI infrastructure is only feasible if underpinned by electricity flowing easily across EU national borders at competitive prices. ECB President Christine Lagarde recently [USN:L1N4560JV TEXT:"warned"] that the bloc faced a choice between missing out on the AI boom entirely or finding itself overly dependent on foreign states – most notably the US and China – for vital technology components. Without progress, the productivity gap with the US will almost certainly widen, EU manufacturing will likely be further undercut by lower-cost Chinese competitors, and the bloc will surely have to continue sourcing critical tech inputs from abroad. The risk-averse EU has long dragged its feet when it comes to reforms, but continuing to do so now may be one of the riskiest moves of all. (The views expressed here are those of Mike Peacock , the former head of communications at the Bank of England and a former senior editor at Reuters.) Enjoying this column? item.title: Bain Capital bets on demand growth for sustainable aviation fuel
item.description: Bain Capital, a major shareholder in sustainable aviation fuel producer EcoCeres, expects blending mandates in several countries will drive long-term growth and sees China requiring it in coming years, a partner at the private equity firm said.
item.dc:creator: Julie Zhu, Kane Wu
item.content:encoded: Bain Capital, a major shareholder in sustainable aviation fuel producer EcoCeres, expects blending mandates in several countries will drive long-term growth and sees China requiring it in coming years, a partner at the private equity firm said. Bain partner James Tam, who is also co-chair of EcoCeres, said in an interview the sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) sector was at the start of a multi-decade expansion as rules for airlines to cut carbon emissions spread from Europe to Asia. "SAF is almost the only commercially available solution to decarbonise aviation," Tam said. "There won't be hydrogen or electric planes for long-haul flights any time soon." The comments come as EcoCeres, the world's second-largest producer of SAF by capacity, prepares a Hong Kong initial public offering that Reuters reported last month could [USN:L1N45G08D TEXT:"raise about $1 billion"]. Tam declined to comment on details of the IPO, which would be a key public market test of investor appetite for pure-play SAF producers. The industry is facing weak demand and has vast spare production capacity, as airlines balk at paying hefty premiums for SAF. The International Air Transport Association said in June an estimated 2.4 million metric tons of SAF will be produced in 2026, "representing just 0.8% of global jet fuel demand and indicating a slowdown in growth", while production capacity is expected to exceed 9 million tons. HONG KONG MANDATE UNDERPINS THIRD PLANT Bain invested more than $700 million in EcoCeres in 2022, when it was the second company after Finland's Neste (NESTE.HE) to commercialise SAF production, Tam said. EcoCeres, which supplies global airlines including Qantas, Air France, British Airways and Cathay Pacific, has combined renewable fuels capacity of about 770,000 metric tons per year at plants in Zhangjiagang in eastern China and [USN:L4N3YO0BM TEXT:"Johor, Malaysia"]. Tam said SAF's inclusion in China's 15th Five-Year Plan signalled that domestic mandates were on the horizon, though exact targets have yet to be announced. The 2026-2030 plan, approved in March, lists SAF among fuels to be developed, but sets no aviation targets. Separately, Hong Kong's [USN:P8N42U0CM TEXT:"first Five-Year Plan"], published in September, targets SAF accounting for 1%-3% of fuel for departing flights in 2030. The plan also backs developing SAF production in Dongguan, Guangdong province, where EcoCeres plans a 450,000-ton-a-year plant, due to open by 2030, to supply airports in Hong Kong, Shenzhen and Guangzhou. Tam said the timeline was firm and the reported HK$10 billion ($1.27 billion) investment covered a 10-year build-out, with the refinery itself costing "meaningfully less." Meeting the top of Hong Kong's target would take nearly half the plant's output, he said. Any surplus could be exported to Europe, where the EU has mandated 6% SAF by 2030. Unlike some rivals, EcoCeres owns its full technology stack and does not rely on third-party technology licensors or catalyst suppliers, giving it a cost advantage, he said. EcoCeres' feedstocks are entirely waste-based, including used cooking oil collected from 500,000 restaurants across China and traceable to each one, a key selling point for airlines. Tam declined to comment on the company's production costs. ($1 = 7.8464 Hong Kong dollars)

item.title: South African rand pressured by stronger dollar, local fuel price hike
item.description: The South African rand was under pressure on Monday, looking to extend a run of four straight weekly losses as a stronger dollar and higher domestic fuel prices weighed on sentiment.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The South African rand was under pressure on Monday, looking to extend a run of four straight weekly losses as a stronger dollar and higher domestic fuel prices weighed on sentiment. At 1449 GMT the rand traded at 16.68 against the dollar , down roughly 0.2% from its previous close The currency has weakened for four consecutive weeks, recording its [USN:L8N45O0GB TEXT:"steepest decline"] last week as a stronger dollar and higher US Treasury yields dampened appetite for emerging-market assets South Africa's government said on Monday that the country's regulated petrol price would [USN:L8N45R0YE TEXT:"rise"] by as much as 12% this week and the wholesale diesel price by 10%, reflecting higher global energy costs linked to the Iran conflict Africa's largest economy imports most of its fuel, leaving it exposed to swings in international oil prices Further weighing on the rand, data showed South Africa's private sector [USN:ZRN00EN0G TEXT:"contracted"] in September at its fastest pace since December as new orders slumped and supply and fuel-related cost pressures intensified On the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, the Top-40 index (.JTOPI) was last down 0.2%. South Africa's benchmark 2035 government bond weakened, as the yield rose 2 basis points to 8.88%

item.title: Italian bank Intesa's improved €35 billion bid for MPS wins backing of biggest investor
item.description: Italy's biggest bank Intesa Sanpaolo has claimed a major victory in its pursuit of Monte dei Paschi di Siena (MPS) by securing the support of its target's largest shareholder for a sweetened takeover offer.
item.dc:creator: Valentina Za
item.content:encoded: Italy's biggest bank Intesa Sanpaolo (ISP.MI) has claimed a major victory in its pursuit of Monte dei Paschi di Siena (MPS) (BMPS.MI) by securing the support of its target's largest shareholder for a sweetened takeover offer. Intesa's €35 billion ($39 billion) bid for MPS is the culmination of hectic consolidation in Italian banking over the past two years. After initially citing antitrust limits for its refusal to join in, Intesa entered the fray in June, just as rival UniCredit (CRDI.MI) closed in on Germany's Commerzbank (CBKG.DE) . MPS had been leading the way until then, having acquired control of bigger rival Mediobanca and become the main investor in Generali (GASI.MI) , Italy's largest insurer and a prized financial asset. To fight Intesa's takeover bid, MPS Chief Executive Luigi Lovaglio drew up a defence plan and called on shareholders to back his strategy in a vote on October 29. MPS has been working on taking Mediobanca private and merging with it, a scheme which will also be put to shareholders on October 29. Lovaglio's plans need the backing of two thirds of the bank's shareholders. Intesa, however, announced late on Sunday that Delfin, the biggest MPS investor with a 17.6% stake, had committed to tendering its stake under Intesa's cash-and-shares bid and to vote against the defence scheme. Support from Delfin, long an ally of MPS chief Lovaglio, was key to the MPS bid defence. However, Delfin now appears to favour the simpler Intesa deal while its own shareholders, the heirs of late Ray-Ban billionaire Leonardo Del Vecchio, are embroiled in legal quarrels over his inheritance. MEDIOBANCA SHARES DIVE Intesa has said it would retain only half of the MPS branch network to address competition concerns, but it would keep the Mediobanca and Generali holdings. Shares in Mediobanca fell as much as 7% on Monday after Intesa urged MPS shareholders to vote against that merger, which would entail a buyout of minorities. Shares in both MPS and Intesa edged higher. Intesa said late on Saturday that it would give [USN:L1N45P04T TEXT:"MPS shareholders a further €800 million"] in cash under its bid if they reject Lovaglio's defence plan. Under Italian takeover rules, investors must authorise any defence strategy that could block a bid. Lovaglio has been trying to cast the vote simply as a way to keep pressure on Intesa. However, Intesa said it would take its offer off the table if MPS shareholders approve the defence strategy. The sweetener raises the bid's cash component of €3 billion by 25% but represents an overall improvement of 2.3% based on the closing price for MPS shares on Friday. ($1 = 0.8939 euros)

item.title: Spain's Sanchez gambles on snap election after housing protests give rare boost
item.description: The snap vote is a high-stakes gamble for Sanchez, whose Socialist Party trails in nearly every opinion poll.
item.dc:creator: Victoria Waldersee, David Latona
item.content:encoded: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Monday called an early election for November 29, aiming to increase his parliamentary support after lawmakers last week [USN:L1N45O0BD TEXT:"rejected"] proposals to address a housing crisis that has drawn nationwide protests. The snap vote is a high-stakes gamble for Sanchez, whose Socialist Party trails in nearly every opinion poll. An electoral defeat would spell the end of one of Europe's last remaining left-leaning governments at a time when the far right is making [USN:L1N45C01D TEXT:"unprecedented gains"] across the region. It reflects a broader malaise across Europe, under pressure from US President Donald Trump on defence spending, cheap Chinese imports, higher borrowing costs, disaffected youth and the biggest surge in support for the far-right since the 1930s. However, Sanchez, a wily political operator, has proven time and again his ability to surprise those who had long written him off. An election now could see him capitalise on a wave of anger at unaffordable housing in Spain. "We need to mobilise and win a much larger progressive majority in parliament, one that will allow us to overcome vested interests, deliver new social advances and continue transforming Spain," Sanchez said in a televised address. Spain's blue-chip index (.IBEX) was flat after the announcement, while Spanish government bonds were broadly steady. OPPOSITION PLEDGES MORE HOMEBUILDING Alberto Nuñez Feijoo, leader of the opposition People's Party, on Monday pledged to almost double homebuilding in Spain to 200,000 units a year and cut taxes if he gained power. “Housing has been this government’s great failure and must be the next one’s success. When a prime minister has been in office for eight years, it is very difficult to blame others for what he has failed to do," Feijoo said at a small business conference. Sanchez has made a name internationally with progressive stances on issues from [USN:L5N3UV09Y TEXT:"Palestinian statehood"] to [USN:L6N41201D TEXT:"defending multilateral institutions"] and cracking down on "[USN:L8N3Z116E TEXT:"tech oligarchs"]", even as a series of scandals weakened his position at home. The recent protests over housing have given him a much-needed fillip, with proposals that were [USN:L1N45O0BD TEXT:"struck down"] by right-wing lawmakers on Friday welcomed by protesters. Polls suggest a coalition led by the PP with the support of anti-immigration Vox is the most likely outcome, which would usher a far-right party into central government for the first time since Spain's return to democracy following the 1975 death of dictator Francisco Franco. PP and Vox would win a combined 203 seats in the lower house, a comfortable majority in the 350-seat chamber, according to a Sigma Dos poll published on Monday in El Mundo newspaper. The Socialists and their junior coalition partners Sumar were projected to win 112 seats. Sanchez has cobbled together a series of fragile coalitions including voices from the far-left to the separatist right to remain in power for eight years. Growing fragmentation among his partners has meant the government has failed to [USN:L8N43P2I6 TEXT:"pass a budget"] and has enacted only a few laws since 2023, even as Spain's economy has continued to outperform the rest of the developed world. Sanchez plans to force through the two housing decrees that were rejected by parliament last week via a rarely used legislative mechanism, according to state broadcaster TVE and newspaper El Pais. When the 350-member chamber is dissolved ahead of an election, a standing body made up of 68 members plus the house speaker remains in place to pass emergency legislation, which has a slim 35-34 majority in favour of the measures. VOX SEES UNPREDICTABLE ELECTION Vox leader Santiago Abascal warned the election result would be unpredictable despite favourable polling for the right. The decision to call a snap election reflected Sanchez's inability to govern without a stable majority, said Miriam Nogueras, parliamentary spokesperson for the Catalan pro-independence party Junts, which in recent years had stopped voting with the government. Sanchez won a second four-year term in office in 2023 after promising a highly controversial amnesty for pro-independence Catalan leaders in exchange for their support, a move still bitterly remembered by many voters as a betrayal of Spanish unity. He won early plaudits for moves including the exhumation of Franco from a mausoleum the dictator built for himself outside Madrid, and a labour law reform that has helped reduce unemployment to its lowest level in almost two decades. He has argued that immigration is essential for sustaining Spanish growth and has refused to agree to US-led demands to increase defence spending to 5% of GDP, angering Trump. Sanchez's housing measures provided a rare chance for him to pitch himself as the leader of a mobilised left and distract from the more politically damaging issues of the migrant crisis in [USN:L1N45A0JO TEXT:"Ceuta"] and corruption scandals, said Lorenzo Bernaldo de Quiros, economist and president of consultancy Freemarket Corporate Intelligence. "This is a window of opportunity," Bernaldo de Quiros said. "If he does not call elections fast, (those topics) will return to centre stage."

item.title: OKX joint venture files with SEC to launch tokenized trading platform
item.description: OKXICE, the joint venture between crypto exchange OKX and Intercontinental Exchange , filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Sunday to launch a tokenized securities platform for around-the-clock trading of US stocks.
item.dc:creator: Gregor Hunter
item.content:encoded: OKXICE, the joint venture between crypto exchange OKX and Intercontinental Exchange (ICE.N) , filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Sunday to launch a tokenized securities platform for around-the-clock trading of US stocks. More than 60 listed companies will be available for around-the-clock trading throughout the week, according to the filing "This is a landmark step toward a truly global, 24/7 Wall Street," said former New York Governor Andrew Cuomo, who is co-chair of OKXICE, in a post on the X social media platform The SEC unveiled an [USN:L6N4590SA TEXT:"exemption"] last month allowing companies to offer trading in blockchain-based or "tokenized" stocks and other securities. The move came two days after comprehensive cryptocurrency legislation backed by US President Donald Trump [USN:L1N4570IP TEXT:"failed to advance"] in the Senate Global exchanges including the NYSE, Nasdaq and the London Stock Exchange are preparing to launch round-the-clock trading in the coming months Prediction markets' push into US stock trading has recently raised [USN:L6N44114G TEXT:"regulatory concerns"]

item.title: European EV sales hit record in 'pivotal' year for affordable cars, study shows
item.description: Europe's uptake of electric vehicles is gaining momentum, with record sales so far this year driven by a slew of affordable models coming onto the market to bring carmakers in line with EU targets, according to a study.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Europe's uptake of electric vehicles is gaining momentum, with record sales so far this year driven by a slew of affordable models coming onto the market to bring carmakers in line with EU targets, according to a study. EV sales across the EU reached record volumes in 2026, with 1.64 million sold in the January-to-August period, up 45% year-on-year, Brussels-based environmental advocacy group Transport & Environment found in its EV progress report published on Monday. EVs made up 22% of the market during this period, six points higher than the same period last year, according to the report. T&E called 2026 "a pivotal year for EV availability", with model choice up 50% in a single year as carmakers expand their line-ups to meet EU emissions targets. The report comes as carmakers like Volkswagen roll out a number of affordable EVs, such as the all-electric Polo, helping the German auto group to close its existing compliance gap and avoid fines. European carmakers dominated the EV offering with nearly 60% of available models, adding 16 in the first half of 2026. Chinese carmakers held 21% and added 11 models. The study also noted the impact of rising fuel prices linked to the Middle East conflict on drivers of combustion-engine cars. Diesel has risen the most, up 38% since the Iran war began, with a 50-litre tank now costing €30 ($34) more, it said. ($1 = €0.8890)

item.title: US stocks mixed, while euro slides on France worries and Brazil markets surge
item.description: US stocks were mixed in early trading on Monday, as easing bets on a Federal Reserve rate hike helped cushion broader market sentiment, although Treasury yields and oil prices remained elevated.
item.dc:creator: Lawrence Delevingne, Danilo Masoni
item.content:encoded: US stocks were mixed in early trading on Monday, as easing bets on a Federal Reserve rate hike helped cushion broader market sentiment, although Treasury yields and oil prices remained elevated. On Wall Street, the Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) fell 0.57%, the S&P 500 (.SPX) rose 0.14%, and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) added about 0.5%. Concerns over France's fiscal position pushed the euro to a 17-month low and weighed on French assets. Europe's pan-regional STOXX 600 (.STOXX) index [USN:L6N45R0EH TEXT:"edged up 0.15%,"] although Paris shares (.FCHI) fell about 1.1% to [USN:L6N45R0EH TEXT:"six-month lows"]. Brazilian stocks rallied after right-wing Senator Flavio [USN:L6N45Q04L TEXT:"Bolsonaro"] outperformed poll predictions in the first round of the presidential election and advanced to a runoff against leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. The iShares MSCI Brazil ETF jumped about 14%, while the Brazilian real [USN:L6N45R0RK TEXT:"surged"] against the dollar as Bolsonaro's lead raised hopes of a more business-friendly policy agenda. MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe (.MIWD00000PUS) rose 0.26%. "Relative equity market calm amid the bond market’s 'perfect storm' is understandable, given accelerating economic growth and the AI boom’s rate insensitivity," Lisa Shalett, chief investment officer of Morgan Stanley Wealth Management, said in an email Monday. Shalett wrote that her team was watching three areas for signs of stress: equity market and earnings revisions breadth; high-yield bond spreads; and US dollar strength along with currency market volatility. FRANCE WEIGHS ON THE EURO The euro recovered some ground to trade at $1.119 after falling by as much as 0.8% to a 17-month low of $1.1160. The single currency, down about 2.5% last month, has come under pressure as [USN:L6N45O0HP TEXT:"investors fret"] over France's rising debt and political gridlock ahead of next year's presidential election. The premium investors demand to hold French 10-year bonds over safer German debt surged above [USN:L8N45O0YO TEXT:"150 basis points"] on Friday, fuelling concerns of broader contagion across European markets. "France is the real deal in terms of risk premia for the euro," said Saxo strategist Neil Wilson, noting that French government plans to reduce the budget deficit still face parliamentary scrutiny and could ultimately be watered down. French 10-year yields stayed below Friday's peak of 4.993%, while German yields were also little changed. The euro's slide lent fresh support to the dollar, which also drew strength from elevated Treasury yields. The dollar index (.DXY) rose 0.4%. While expectations of a Fed pause could weigh on the dollar, "US growth outperformance and strong foreign appetite for US securities keep US dollar risks skewed to the upside," said Elias Haddad, global head of markets strategy at BBH. Benchmark 10-year US Treasury yields ticked up 2.5 basis points to 5.3%, while two-year yields slipped 0.66 basis points to 4.818%. Still, borrowing costs across major economies remain near multi-year highs as deteriorating public finances, heavy debt issuance and elevated energy prices continue to pressure bond markets. FED REPRICING OFFERS SUPPORT Trading was thin in Asia due to holidays in China and South Korea as well as in Australia's New South Wales state, though regional markets took their cue from Wall Street's gains on Friday after weaker-than-expected US labor data. Figures released last week showed [USN:L1N45N170 TEXT:"US job growth"] slowed more than expected in September and payrolls for the previous two months were revised sharply lower, prompting investors to largely rule out a Federal Reserve rate increase this month. Japan's Nikkei (.N225) rose 2.4% and MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan (.MISX00000PUS) rose 1.2%. Investors now see an 18% chance of a Fed rate increase this month, down from 64% a week ago, according to CME FedWatch data, though a move in December remains largely priced in. Oil prices fell in volatile trade as concerns about potential supply disruptions linked to the US-Israeli war on Iran were balanced by the impact of rising Middle East exports and a Group of Seven pledge to boost supplies. Brent crude futures dropped 0.65% to $101.57 a barrel, while US crude was down 1.5% at $89.70. Spot gold was little changed at $4,141 an ounce.

item.title: India-China thaw faces major economic tests
item.description: India is working to emerge from China’s shadow while improving diplomatic relations, but the more the world’s most populous country pushes, the more apparent its dependence on its wealthier neighbour becomes.
item.dc:creator: Manishi Raychaudhuri
item.content:encoded: India is working to emerge from China’s shadow while [USN:L6N4500OX TEXT:"improving diplomatic relations"], but the more the world’s most populous country pushes, the more apparent its dependence on its wealthier neighbour becomes. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping [USN:P8N44B08W TEXT:"met in New Delhi"] last month, Xi's first visit to the subcontinent in seven years. The two leaders pledged to rebuild ties badly damaged by [USN:L1N3M10AB TEXT:"deadly hand-to-hand troop clashes in 2020"] on their shared but ill-defined Himalayan border. There are other signs of warming relations since the two Asian giants last year [USN:FWN3M01QR TEXT:"agreed to end the military standoff"]. [USN:L4N3UB0D6 TEXT:"Direct flights"] between Indian and Chinese cities have resumed after being suspended since the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, and visa services in China have expanded. But such measures only go so far. Long-standing trade dependence and strategic mistrust will not be addressed with handshakes and plane flights. The two Asian giants’ economic relationship remains deeply asymmetric. China's share of global value-added manufacturing stood at 28% in 2025, dwarfing India's 3%, according to the World Bank. The export picture is just as lopsided for India. China’s 16.3% share of global merchandise exports in 2025 massively surpasses India’s 1.7% . Moreover, India imported goods worth $116 billion more from China than it exported in 2025. By August this year, the deficit had already hit $91 billion and was on track to surpass last year's record. CAPTIVE SUPPLY CHAINS The problem is not only that India imports more from China. It is also that many of those imports are indispensable to Indian industry. Electrical and electronic equipment, machinery, and chemicals – the three largest import categories – are largely intermediate goods used by domestic manufacturers. The more India exports, the more it needs to import from China. Smartphones and generic medicines illustrate the dilemma. India has made progress in assembling electronics and expanding pharmaceutical production, but many of the components and inputs needed for both sectors still come from China. This intense reliance has many broad strategic implications. For example, Beijing's [USN:L4N3R10B3 TEXT:"imposition of export licensing"] requirements on seven heavy rare earths in April 2025 exposed [USN:L4N3SI03M TEXT:"vulnerabilities in India’s automotive"] and defense manufacturing sectors. Of course, some of India’s manufacturing weakness is primarily homegrown. The country’s research and development spending stood at just 0.64% of gross domestic product in 2024, according to the most recent Economic Survey, sharply lower than that of Asian peers, partly because of private-sector underinvestment. Skilled-labour shortages compound the problem. Foxconn's (2317.TW) [USN:L6N3UZ072 TEXT:"withdrawal of Chinese staff"] from its Indian iPhone factories in 2025 illustrated how dependent advanced manufacturing can be on foreign technical expertise. INDIA’S FIXES New Delhi is seeking to address the imbalance. [USN:FWN3ZY0TT TEXT:"India recently relaxed restrictions"] on foreign direct investment (FDI) from Chinese companies, allowing them to take up to a 10% stake in Indian firms. The government simultaneously announced fast-track clearance of investment proposals in five high-technology areas within 60 days, with the stipulation that they must be structured as joint ventures with majority Indian ownership. On top of this, Indian exports to China rose by 40% between April and August. Industrial machinery, automotive components, printed circuit boards, smartphones and other electronics have driven much of that increase. But the export surge should not be mistaken for a fundamental shift in the relationship. Much of India's electronics growth still depends on imported Chinese components. Smartphone manufacturing — India’s biggest export success story — remains only 18-20% locally sourced. Northeast Asia’s AI boom appears to be generating positive spillovers for the subcontinent, with Indian firms picking up sub-component work from Chinese tech giants facing surging hardware demand. But, again, this dynamic reinforces the centrality of Chinese supply chains. TRUST DEFICIT PERSISTS For India-bound Chinese FDI and technology transfer to materialise, one question needs to be answered: what does India bring to the table? The obvious answers are access to a large market and a young, low-cost labour pool as well as New Delhi's various incentives to spur industrial growth — including tax breaks, production-linked payouts, and capital subsidies — but China doesn't appear to be taking the bait. China’s pressure on its leading companies to withhold critical technologies illustrates how protective Beijing is about its most sophisticated capabilities — electric vehicles (EVs), batteries, solar energy and electronic equipment. Meanwhile, the 3,800-km (2,400-mile) disputed border in the Himalayas continues to cast a shadow over the relationship. A gradual, multi-year [USN:P8N42604N TEXT:"stabilisation strategy"] is in place — diplomats met in Beijing in August pledging a "fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable settlement" — but a final resolution doesn't appear imminent . For now, both governments appear willing to give economic cooperation more room. But India's challenge is not simply to import less from China. It is to use renewed engagement with its neighbour to build its own domestic capabilities. Until then, the relationship between Asia’s two largest economies will remain decidedly one-sided. (The views expressed here are those of Manishi Raychaudhuri , the founder and CEO of Emmer Capital Partners Ltd and the former head of Asia-Pacific Equity Research at BNP Paribas Securities.) item.title: Rubio, asked about US bombers leaving UK, says no direct link with suspected plot
item.description: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday there was no direct link between the sudden removal of his country's bombers from a British airbase and a suspected Iranian plot at the site last week.
item.dc:creator: Kate Holton, Jonathan Landay
item.content:encoded: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday there was no direct link between the sudden removal of his country's bombers from a British airbase and a suspected Iranian plot at the site last week. The planes had been stationed at RAF Fairford, the preferred European base for US bombers, and had recently been used in US strikes on Iran. Last week five British men were arrested near the base - which Iran's Revolutionary Guards previously said was a legitimate target - on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. "I wouldn't just directly tie that to the move that was made," Rubio told reporters, when asked about the B1 bombers. "The Department of War is constantly reallocating resources where they need to be." A NATO military source had said on Monday: "It is still believed that Iran poses an acute threat to US assets in the UK". While much about [USN:L1N45O076 TEXT:"the incident remains unexplained"], British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said any plot was likely backed by [USN:L1N45O076 TEXT:"Iran"]. Iran has said accusations that it was involved in any plot are baseless, and Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi wrote on X: "I can confirm Iran's belief that releasing supposed terrorists working for foreign states really says it all. You're barking up the wrong tree." KEY AIR BASE FOR US STRIKES Rubio said on Monday the US had confidence in the security of all its bases. Fairford, located 90 miles (145 km) west of London, is one of the most important in Europe for the US, being one of only a few suitable for heavy bombers such as the B1 aircraft. It has played a key role in previous US campaigns in the Middle East, although its bombers are not stationed there permanently. During the current conflict, the US had permission to use Fairford only to strike Iranian missile sites that were attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz, or so-called defensive strikes. London had refused permission for the US to use British bases for offensive strikes on Iran. That approach has strained ties between the US and Britain, typically one of Washington's closest allies. A Pentagon official confirmed on Sunday that all US bombers which had been deployed to Fairford had headed to their home stations in the US. The Pentagon said the US bomber force remained ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities "anywhere, anytime". The New York Times, citing two US officials, said the US had rushed over the weekend to move the bombers after commanders received new threats about an Iran-backed plot. It said some of the planes had left while aerial refuelling aircraft were still being scrambled. A US official declined to comment. The British government also declined to comment, although a spokesman for Burnham said the base was safe. Christoph Bergs, research analyst at defence think tank the Royal United Services Institute, said the redeployment would in the short term reduce the US' capacity "to quickly surge sorties against Iran, reducing the threat level somewhat". But he noted that use of Fairford was already limited given London's stipulation on defensive strikes. The aircraft could now potentially be sent to either Diego Garcia or bases in the Gulf, to reduce the need for more air-to-air refuelling to cover the additional distance, but that would depend on capacity availability, negotiations with allies and security, he added. PLOT WAS FOR 'BIG DAMAGE' In the early hours of September 27, five British men in their 20s were arrested after being seen running into fields from three white vans parked near the base. Police said no explosive devices were found but a quantity of petrol was present. The men have since been [USN:L1N45P02S TEXT:"released on bail"]. A sixth man, a dual UK-Iranian national arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts four days later, has also been released on bail. US President Donald Trump said at the time of the first arrests that the plot had [USN:L1N45J01J TEXT:"planned "big damage""] and that it might have been connected to Iran. Trump later said he would not have [USN:L1N45K087 TEXT:"released"] the suspects on bail. A senior NATO military official said the removal of the bombers would have no impact on the alliance: "NATO's defensive agility towards any aggression remains unchanged and unmatched thanks to the unity, strength, and combined capabilities of 32 nations." The Wall Street Journal first reported the removal of the US bombers.

item.title: Schneider Electric to buy US software firm PTC in $22.6 billion deal
item.description: France's Schneider Electric struck its biggest deal ever on Monday, agreeing to buy US software company PTC for around $22.6 billion as it builds up its data centre business amid booming demand.
item.dc:creator: Sabrina Valle, Lucie Barbier, Dimitri Rhodes
item.content:encoded: France's Schneider Electric (SCHN.PA) struck its biggest deal ever on Monday, agreeing to buy US software company PTC (PTC.O) for around $22.6 billion as it builds up its data centre business amid booming demand. However, the French engineering company's shares fell nearly 10% in early Paris trading as investors weighed the size of the acquisition, the big premium offered for the shares and the outlook for software companies' valuations amid AI-related market uncertainty. Up to Friday's close, Schneider's shares were up 29% year-to-date, before Monday's losses wiped off close to €15 billion ($17 billion) from its market capitalisation. "AI disruption fears are still weighing on software valuations, which allows acquiring PTC at a decade low valuation but could still weigh on Schneider post deal," Jefferies said in a note to investors. Berenberg analyst Nay Soe Naing told Reuters the deal presented a healthy valuation amid a compressed valuation environment and challenging investor sentiment across the software space. PTC shares jumped 34.4% in US premarket trading. BACKBONE OF DATA CENTRE BUILD-UP Schneider, once known primarily for industrial components like fuses and circuit breakers, now builds the backbone of data centres, supplying everything from cooling units and server racks to critical power distribution equipment. The PTC acquisition would expand its industrial software and AI business by adding the Boston-based company's product-design and lifecycle-management software to its offering. Schneider CEO Olivier Blum told investors that PTC's engineering and design data would strengthen Schneider's ability to deploy AI across customers' industrial operations. "Data is becoming a very critical layer" for extracting value from AI, as the technology requires closer links between data and the software used to contextualise it, Blum said in the conference call. The combination would lift Schneider's software-as-a-service revenue to about 24% of group total, accelerating its push beyond electrical equipment and automation into higher-growth, recurring-revenue software, he added. Booming demand for data centres, particularly from the US, is driving [USN:L6N41D0F0 TEXT:"Schneider's earnings"], offering a growing source of revenue that is helping it offset weakness in some traditional electrical-equipment markets. PTC, which provides software solutions for designing, manufacturing and servicing products across multiple sectors, has also [USN:L4N43V2I2 TEXT:"benefited"] from growing demand for its AI-powered tools. Monday's deal follows Schneider's June agreement to buy [USN:L6N432112 TEXT:"Cognite Holding"], a privately held provider of AI software and industrial data. DEAL DETAILS The transaction would be Schneider's largest-ever acquisition and one of the biggest in Europe this year, according to LSEG data. It would be financed through an issuance of new shares worth €5 billion to €6 billion under an existing shareholder authorisation, and new debt of €16 billion to €17 billion. The $205-per-share offer implies an enterprise value of $23.7 billion for PTC and represents a 42.3% premium to its last closing price. France's third-highest-valued listed company expects the deal to generate €250 million in annual run-rate cost savings by the third year after closing, alongside about €800 million in revenue synergies. The acquisition is expected to close by the third quarter of 2027, subject to approvals from PTC shareholders and regulators. ($1 = €0.8929)

item.title: Bolsonaro will face Lula in runoff in Brazil's presidential vote
item.description: Right-wing Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro exceeded expectations in Sunday's first-round vote with a slight lead over the incumbent.
item.dc:creator: Luciana Magalhaes, Lisandra Paraguassu, Ricardo Brito, Brendan O'Boyle
item.content:encoded: Right-wing Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro will face leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in a runoff of the presidential election later this month, after he exceeded expectations in Sunday's first-round vote with a slight lead over the incumbent. The election, which centered around the [USN:L6N459162 TEXT:"cost of living"], corruption and insecurity in Brazilians' daily lives, follows a string of wins across Latin America by right-wing parties aligned with US President Donald Trump. Bolsonaro's stronger-than-expected performance, at 47% of votes versus Lula's 45%, is expected to buoy his campaign and may bolster Brazil's currency and stock market, which have risen on the prospects of the business-friendly challenger. Private surveys in the run-up to the election had forecast Lula leading the first-round vote by around 3 percentage points. "Brazil wants change and I am very happy with the results," Bolsonaro told reporters in Brasilia after nearly all tallies were reported, heralding "the end of the era of (Lula's) Workers' Party." The senator, son of [USN:L1N45F0NC TEXT:"right-wing former President"] Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year [USN:S0N3UJ08N TEXT:"sentence"] for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election, now heads to an October 25 showdown with the [USN:L1N45G04J TEXT:"leftist Lula"]. Addressing a crowd at a hotel in Sao Paulo, Lula said he had been convinced he would win the election in the first round. "Starting tomorrow, we begin a new campaign," he said, promising to show voters what he had accomplished as president. Despite growing worries over Brazil's public finances and sluggish economic growth, the campaign offered [USN:L1N4580UE TEXT:"meager policy debate"], as both leading candidates skipped the major TV debates. SURPRISE SHOWING "The pollsters missed badly," said Robert Muggah, cofounder of think-tank Igarape Institute. "Expect the runoff polls, which show a dead heat, to understate Bolsonaro as well." Early on Sunday, Bolsonaro told journalists in Rio de Janeiro he was counting on "a protest vote from people who would otherwise vote for another candidate but are opposed to Lula." Thaise Lima, a 41-year-old lawyer on her way to vote in Sao Paulo, said her main goal was to get Lula's Workers' Party out of office. "I don't think Flavio is the best candidate, but I might decide to vote for him in the next few minutes," she said, adding that she wished psychiatrist and author Augusto Cury were a more viable candidate. Fernando Tempel, 49, a management consultant, told Reuters he was voting for Bolsonaro despite initially planning to vote for Romeu Zema, the former governor of Minas Gerais state. "The protest vote foreshadows what is to come in the runoff," said political analyst Rafael Favetti. "While this should benefit Flavio Bolsonaro now, his growth potential in the second round drops precisely because that support has already been front-loaded." ECONOMIC HEADWINDS Despite Brazil's [USN:L1N44111S TEXT:"falling inequality"] and unemployment, Lula has struggled to win over voters grappling with the high cost of living, heavy household debt and the threat of crime and more pervasive gang activity. Bolsonaro has sought to capitalize on cost-of-living concerns, while Lula moved to ban online gambling and, as the race tightened, expanded welfare and proposed fresh debt relief for families. Rising spending and public debt above 82% of GDP have stoked fiscal concerns that Brazil's next president will need to address. The government lowered its [USN:L1N45E0QC TEXT:"economic growth forecasts"] for this year and next to 2.0% and 2.3%, respectively. "I voted for Brazil to start growing again," said Marciano de Souza e Silva, a 52-year-old public servant in Brasilia who voted for Flavio. OVERSHADOWED DEBATE Scandals and fears of foreign interference ahead of the vote largely overshadowed policy debates during the campaign. Controversy surrounding the now-defunct Banco Master engulfed much of Brazil's political class after Daniel Vorcaro, who ran the bank, was arrested earlier this year and accused of a multibillion-dollar fraud scheme, which he denies. A federal police investigation has looked into the banker's ties to figures across Brazil's political elite, including Bolsonaro, who is being [USN:L1N4530BQ TEXT:"investigated for "][USN:L1N4530BQ TEXT:"suspected money "][USN:L1N4530BQ TEXT:"laundering"] that police have tied to the case. Bolsonaro has denied wrongdoing. Throughout the campaign, Lula's allies have warned that the Trump administration might refuse to recognize election results if he wins, pointing to an aborted effort to [USN:L6N43R03C TEXT:"send US officials to Brazil"]. Trump has not formally endorsed a candidate, though he hosted Senator Bolsonaro at the White House and praised him publicly. Reuters reported on Wednesday that Brazilian intelligence officials briefed a French and German delegation on [USN:L1N45E08V TEXT:"alleged US and Russian interference"] before the election. The US has rejected claims of interference in Brazil's affairs. On Sunday afternoon, Brazil's electoral court chief Kassio Nunes Marques said the election was running smoothly.

item.title: Revolut's rise to become Europe's $115 billion big bank rival
item.description: Revolut has become Europe's most valuable startup and a challenge to centuries-old banking giants, though it faces hurdles.
item.dc:creator: Lawrence White, Elizabeth Howcroft
item.content:encoded: Revolut has risen to become Europe's most valuable startup and a challenge to centuries-old banking giants, having grown rapidly since it was launched just over a decade ago as a fintech promising cheaper forex fees. Yet Revolut faces many hurdles itself, with the amount of revenue it extracts per customer a fraction of its established competitors and a small lending business by industry standards. A spokesperson for Revolut said in an email that the London-based company has a "diversified business model", earning its revenue from various products and services rather than lending. "That means our growth depends on building things customers value, rather than on interest rates," the spokesperson said. Here's Revolut's rise, in five charts: GOING FOR GLOBAL CEO Nik Storonsky has stressed he wants Revolut to be truly global, expanding into markets [USN:L4N44E0AO TEXT:"from Mexico to Australia"]. The company has announced several new licences in recent weeks, as it aims to become one of only a handful of banks with retail operations spanning so much of the globe. Meanwhile, some traditional lenders seen as global, including HSBC (HSBA.L) , are reducing their retail footprint. Valued at $115 billion privately, Revolut is now worth more than Britain's Barclays (BARC.L) and France's Societe Generale (SOGN.PA) as investors bet on its tech platform winning over more customers globally. Revolut's 2025 pretax profit was £1.7 billion ($2.2 billion), a fraction of Barclays' £9 billion, but growing fast. Paulo Macedo, CEO of Portugal's biggest bank, Caixa Geral de Depósitos, said in June that 2025 was the last year in which the 150-year-old bank would record higher profit than Revolut. "When you go to Europe the bank CEOs there are talking about Revolut as their most important threat because of their aggressive marketing and growth," said Cihan Duran, director at S&P Global Ratings. MARRED BY SETBACKS In the US, where Revolut has a provisional license, it will face tougher competition, investors said. "The US could be potentially the biggest growth for Revolut. But at the same time, the US is the most competitive market," said Konstantin Sidorov, CEO of the London Technology Club, which invested in Revolut when it was valued at just $5.5 billion. There have been setbacks, including a fine in Lithuania for failing to prevent money laundering. Revolut said an investigation had not identified any confirmed instances of money laundering, adding that it had signed a settlement with the central bank and taken steps to resolve shortcomings. And in September, Revolut accidentally sent customer data to hackers posing as government investigators. The company said its systems and customer funds were unaffected and it had contacted the "limited number of impacted individuals" to give support. In 2024 and 2025, Revolut was the most-complained-about bank in Britain in fraud cases whereby customers are tricked into sending cash to scammers, Ombudsman data compiled by consumer advocacy firm Which? showed. Revolut has previously said in response it takes fraud very seriously and has robust customer protections in place. CUSTOMERS HAVE SURGED A striking measure of its growth is customer numbers. In Ireland, for example, Revolut said that 80% of the adult population has a Revolut account. Revolut's website shows it has 80 million customers, against 84 million for JPMorgan (JPM.N) and 41 million for HSBC. REVENUE-PER-CUSTOMER IS LOW Revolut makes far less from each of its customers than traditional banks, a Reuters analysis of its figures shows. Average deposit balances are also much lower. Lower per-customer revenue is in part because Revolut lends much less than traditional banks, instead relying on fees such as card subscriptions. With just £2.2 billion in loans at end-2025, Revolut's loan-to-deposit ratio of 6% compares with 55% for HSBC and 86% for Societe Generale. Scaling its lending business will introduce risks including managing big and complex credit exposures, while entering fiercely competitive local mortgage markets will not be easy, analysts and investors said. TOO FEW PRIMARY ACCOUNTS Revolut has attracted customers with its easy-to-use app but executives acknowledge too few use it as a primary bank account. Revolut declined to comment in its latest results on how many customers did so in 2025, but said the figure was up 45% from a year ago. This metric is a focus for Revolut's biggest backers. Alex Immerman, an investor at Andreessen Horowitz, which is known as "a16z", told Reuters it was watching for primary-account adoption, as well as total customer balances. ($1 = 0.7573 pounds)
